ch17.anchor: Shen Anna, died in Beijing at the age of ninety-five
ch17.note: Shen Anna (1915–2010), born Shen Wan, was the Communists’ long-planted stenographer inside the Nationalist high command, taking down its most secret conferences in shorthand for more than a decade; her story, and that of her husband Hua Mingzhi, is told in Chapter Thirteen.

The people named in this long paragraph are the children, grandchildren, and other kin of the Central Special Branch figures the book has told of—among them Zhou Enlai, Chen Yun, Bo Gu, Chen Geng, Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, Pan Hannian, and Dong Jianwu—whom the author consulted while researching it.

ch17.anchor: This too I learned from Mr. Yang Tianshi.
ch17.note: Yang Tianshi (b. 1936) is one of China’s most eminent historians of the Republican period, a research fellow of the Institute of Modern History at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and best known abroad for his work on Chiang Kai-shek’s diaries.

ch17.anchor: To know what you know and to know what you do not know
ch17.note: From the Analects of Confucius: “When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it—this is knowledge.”

The Yanshi Jiaxun (Family Instructions for the Yan Clan), written in the sixth century by Yan Zhitui, is the earliest surviving Chinese book of family precepts; its chapter “Exhortation to Study” is a classic statement of scholarly caution. The “correcting brush” renders cihuang, orpiment, the yellow mineral once painted over a manuscript to blot out and amend a character.
